𝐖𝐞𝐛 𝐋𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐭𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫 – 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐩𝐭𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐒𝐭𝐞𝐞𝐥 𝐆𝐢𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧 (𝐀𝐀𝐒𝐇𝐓𝐎 𝐋𝐑𝐅𝐃)
Continuing from my previous post on vertical stiffeners,
https://lnkd.in/dy7KY8He
which received strong engagement, today I would like to share some practical insights the web longitudinal stiffener (LS)

1️⃣ 𝐏𝐮𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐫𝐨𝐥𝐞
✔ Longitudinal stiffeners are stability members, not primary load-carrying elements.
 ✔ Their main function is to prevent or delay web bend-buckling by restraining out-of-plane deformation of the web.
 ✔ They are not mandatory in every steel girder and are used only when web stability requirements cannot be satisfied without them.

2️⃣ 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐟𝐢𝐠𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐞𝐭𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠
✔ Longitudinal stiffeners are placed in the compression zone of the web, acting as ribs welded along the girder axis.
✔ Longitudinal stiffeners are usually interrupted at vertical stiffeners, or require coping / openings if continuous.
✔ Common stiffener shapes: 
 • Plate – most common, simple.
 • Lor T-sections – used when higher stiffness is required 
✔ Common practice: 1 stiffener → located at 0.2H from the compression flange, 2 stiffeners → located at about 0.15H and 0.35H

3️⃣ 𝐃𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧 𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐞𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐀𝐀𝐒𝐇𝐓𝐎 𝐋𝐑𝐅𝐃

3.1 Shear resistance
❌ In AASHTO, long stiffeners do NOT directly increase the nominal shear resistance of the web.
 → However, stiffeners indirectly affect shear design by changing the classification of the web panel.

✔ An interior web panel is considered stiffened if:
W/o long stiffeners → transverse stiffener spacing ≤ 3D, or
With one or more long stiffeners → transverse stiffener spacing ≤ 2D (in 10th Edition, 2024)  ⚠(this limit was 1.5D in earlier editions).

🤔 This rule may look illogical at first.
 In reality: A long stiffener does not always work. It is effective only when the web panel is short enough. If the panel is long (> 2D), the web can buckle in a pattern that bypasses the stiffener.
 ➡ For this reason, AASHTO does not credit the stiffener in shear design when the spacing is large.

3.2 Web bend-buckling resistance
✔ Under flexural loading, the web is subjected to longitudinal compression and may buckle out of plane.
 ✔ In this case, tension-field action is not available, and the longitudinal stiffener becomes the primary stabilizing element.
📌 AASHTO accounts for this effect in the web bend-buckling resistance equations:

For webs with a single long stiffener, the resistance depends on ds​ (the distance from the comp flange to the stiffener)
For multiple longitudinal stiffeners: not yet provided in AASHTO. Although many studies exist, they have not been adopted in the Spec.

For practical and conservative design, ds​ may be taken as the distance from the compression flange to the centroid of the longitudinal stiffener group.

Today I read the news: a building under construction in Hong Kong caught fire, and the bamboo scaffolding was seemingly the cause.
Deep down I know it’s only a matter of time. This “natural masterpiece of strength” will eventually be phased out and replaced by aluminium and steel.
But when I think about it, I totally get why bamboo scaffolding has survived until today.

1. The fibers run perfectly straight from bottom to top
Unlike most wood where the grain twists, curls and grows sideways, bamboo’s fibers go almost 100% straight along the length of the pole. That gives it incredible tensile strength (sometimes even stronger than regular construction steel) and amazing flexibility.
Years later when we invented carbon fiber, we realized: hey, bamboo is basically a natural carbon-fiber composite.

2. Hollow tube with evenly spaced nodes
It’s hollow inside (just like the steel tubes we design today) so it’s light yet strong. Those nodes you see every 30–50 cm. They act exactly like reinforcement plates or stiffeners, preventing the pole from buckling or crumpling under load.

3. Friction joints
No nails, no bolts, no welding. Just tie them really tight with rope and the rough surface of the bamboo grips each other like crazy. The whole scaffold stays rock solid thanks to that friction. Most people have no idea how strong those simple ties actually are.

4. Insanely fast growth
Because it only grows upward, has a thin outer wall and is hollow inside, bamboo is probably the fastest-growing structural material on the planet. Some species grow nearly a meter a day.

5. Super light, easy to carry, easy to cut and shape on site
You can lift a 6-meter pole with one hand, cut it with a normal saw, and two workers can put up bamboo scaffolding many times faster than metal, no heavy machines needed.

So many of our “great inventions” in materials and construction that started in the West (where bamboo basically doesn’t grow) were us trying to solve problems that bamboo had already solved millions of years ago:
move material far from the neutral axis → hollow tube
prevent local buckling → add nodes/stiffeners
better connections → rough surface for friction
super-strong fibers in one direction → hello carbon fiber

We spent over a century and billions of dollars inventing things that bamboo has been quietly doing since prehistoric times.
So yes, fires like today’s are scary and dangerous, and one day bamboo scaffolding will probably disappear from Hong Kong’s skyline.
But until then, I just have to smile: nature got there first… by a few million years.

When we look at the bamboo scaffolding around tall buildings in Hong Kong, we can notice something interesting. Unlike modern steel scaffolding, which usually has diagonal braces in almost every small frame, bamboo scaffolding often does not use diagonal braces in each small bay. Instead, it uses large diagonal braces that run across big areas of the whole system. 

As a structural engineer, the question is: Why do these diagonal braces exist?

1. From school, we learned a special fact about triangles. A triangle is the stiffest and most stable shape in 2D geometry. If we know all three side lengths, the shape of the triangle is completely fixed. Even if we rotate, flip, or move it, the triangle keeps the same shape. 

2. Later, when we learn about materials, we understand that most materials are much stronger in tension and compression than in bending. To increase bending strength, we need to place material far from the neutral axis. A triangle naturally does this. If we try to bend one side of a triangle, we must stretch or compress the other two sides. This makes the triangle very stiff and hard to deform. 

3. In structural engineering, we learn the formula for a perfect truss: 
m = 2j − 3, where m - the number of members and j - the number of joints.
Only a triangle satisfies this condition of stability: 3 = 2×3 − 3. This means the triangle is the basic stable unit of all truss systems. 

4. In structural mechanics, we also learn about Degrees of Freedom (DOF). Every node in 2D has 2 DOF (movement in x and y). 
A triangle has 3 nodes → 6 DOF total. A triangle has 3 rigid sides → 3 distance constraints. So the remaining DOF is 6 − 3 = 3. These 3 DOF are: translation in X and Y, and rotation of the whole shape. These are rigid-body movements, so the triangle cannot deform inside the plane. 
For a square: 4 nodes → 8 DOF, and only 4 constraints. The remaining DOF is 8 − 4 = 4. After removing 3 rigid-body DOF, the square still has 1 extra DOF, which is shear deformation. This is why a square can easily change into a parallelogram. 

So, the triangle is the only 2D polygon that cannot change shape. This simple fact is the foundation of all structural systems today. Every safe structure depends on triangles. 
Scaffolding needs diagonal braces to create triangles. 
Truss bridges are built from many triangles. 
Tower cranes are made from triangular modules. 
Building frames and many everyday structures need cross-bracing to form triangles and prevent sway. 

In Hong Kong, bamboo scaffolding also follows this rule. The large diagonal braces, usually at 45–60 degrees, connect the vertical poles with the horizontal members. These braces divide the frames they pass through into many small triangles, and also create big triangles at the global scale. Because of these large diagonal braces, the whole scaffolding system becomes much more stable and gains strong resistance against deformation and sway.

Why Metro Viaducts Usually Use:
✔ Concrete Bridges
✔ Box Girders
✔ Segmental Construction

𝟭. 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗿𝗲𝘁𝗲?

- High mass & stiffness → smoother ride: Concrete is heavier and stiffer, so it reduces vibration and noise, even at high metro speeds. This makes the train quieter and more comfortable, especially in cities.
- Better fatigue resistance: Metro trains run very often. Concrete handles millions of repeated loads better than steel, which can crack from fatigue.
- Longer life and lower cost : Concrete does not rust, needs less maintenance, and has good fire resistance. Over the whole life of the bridge, it is much cheaper than steel.

𝟮. 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗕𝗼𝘅 𝗚𝗶𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀?

Box girders act like closed tubes. This shape gives several important advantages:
- High torsional rigidity: It resists twisting very well—important for curved metro tracks.
- High bending capacity: Strong enough for heavy and fast metro trains.
- Even stress distribution: Reduces cracking, increases durability.
- Space inside the girder: Box girders allow space for cables, drainage, and inspection walkways, making maintenance easier.

𝟯. 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗦𝗲𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻?

Unless it's absolutely necessary to span long distances, around 50 meters or less, the Segmental Construction offers many significant advantages over other methods.

A. Fast Construction
- Precast production in a controlled yard enables continuous, high-quality segment fabrication. With the short-line method, production capacity can be easily scaled by adding more casting beds.
- Rapid erection using a launching girder (LG) places segments directly into final position. Although LG equipment is costly, metro viaducts typically consist of hundreds of repetitive spans; therefore the equipment investment is amortized over many uses, resulting in low 

B. Very High Geometric Accuracy
For high-speed metro operation, geometric precision is critical. During segment erection, the coordinate of each segment can be fine-tuned in both vertical and horizontal before post-tensioning. This allows the completed girder to achieve millimeter-level accuracy in profile and plan, which is difficult to achieve with cast-in-place or other construction methods.

C. Reduced Girder Depth
Compared with methods such as balanced cantilever construction, which require the girder to resist large temporary construction loads, resulting in oversized sections—especially near the piers—that are heavier and more expensive than necessary for service conditions.

In precast segmental construction, however, the girder is designed only for in-service loads, because all erection loads are carried by the launching girder (LG). As a result, the girder can be made significantly shallower and more efficient.
Across hundreds of repetitive metro spans, this reduction in girder depth and concrete volume leads to substantial savings in overall cost.

In steel girder bridges, we often focus on the main components such as flanges carrying compression and tension, and the web carrying shear.

However, there are smaller details that play a critical role in the capacity and performance of these main members — web stiffeners.

In this series, I’ll discuss web stiffeners in steel girder bridges—practical lessons rarely taught in classrooms.
(Next post: longitudinal stiffeners.)

🔹 1. Why vertical web stiffeners matter Vertical web stiffeners are not just added plates.

• 𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗯
 Under shear, the web develops diagonal tension and compression. Vertical stiffeners reduce web panel size, act like vertical struts, and help prevent local buckling, allowing the web to carry much higher shear forces.

• 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗳𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲
 Compression flanges tend to rotate and move laterally.  Stiffeners help restrain this movement and reduce the risk of local flange buckling.

• 𝗜𝗻𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝗰𝘂𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗱𝗴𝗲𝘀
 In curved steel bridges, stiffeners welded to both top and bottom flanges connect the flanges together and improve resistance to torsion.

• 𝗥𝗲𝗱𝘂𝗰𝗲 𝗳𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗲𝗹𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀
 Repeated traffic loads cause local rotation between the web and flange.
 Properly detailed stiffeners limit this movement and help reduce fatigue stresses.

🔹 2. Detailing considerations

• 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗴𝗶𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 
 Stiffeners are usually welded to the compression flange, but not to the tension flange, to avoid stress concentration and fatigue cracking.

• 𝗖𝘂𝗿𝘃𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻-𝗰𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗴𝗶𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀
 Stiffeners are often welded to both flanges to improve torsional stiffness and section stability.

• 𝗕𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀
 Stiffeners commonly serve as connection points for bracing between adjacent girders and must be sufficiently stiff to transfer forces. So, it must be welded to flanges

• 𝗕𝗼𝘁𝘁𝗼𝗺 𝗳𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴
 Unless structurally required, stiffeners should stop short of the bottom flange to avoid water traps and corrosion, especially in weathering steel bridges.

🔹 3. Design perspective

• 𝗘𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆
 For slender webs, adding vertical stiffeners can increase shear capacity by about 2–5 times due to tension-field action. (see figure). Typical stiffener spacing ranges from 1.5 to 5.0 m, with closer spacing near supports.

• 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗲 𝗽𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗼𝘀𝗼𝗽𝗵𝘆
 AASHTO requires a projecting width check for stiffeners to prevent local buckling based on experimental evidence. 
 Eurocode, in contrast, allows buckling and accounts for reduced effectiveness.
 This reflects two different design philosophies:
 prevent buckling (AASHTO) vs. allow buckling with reduced capacity (Eurocode).

𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐡𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐨𝐧 𝐚 𝐭𝐚𝐩𝐞 𝐦𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐟𝐢𝐱𝐞𝐝

That’s not a defect — it’s smart engineering.
The hook is designed to 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵 by exactly the thickness of the metal hook itself. 
This allows the tape measure to stay accurate in two different situations:
✔ Pulling from an edge → true outside measurement
✔ Pushing against a wall → true inside measurement

Smart design. Zero error. 👌

𝗪𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗔𝗜 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗖𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗹 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝘀?

When I chose to study civil engineering, it was still a “hot” major. Infrastructure was growing fast and bridges, roads, and high-rise buildings were being built everywhere. 
But by the time I graduated, the IT industry was booming. Software engineers had much higher salaries and more opportunities. Many times I wondered what would have happened if I had chosen computer science instead.
Then a few years later, AI exploded. AI engineers became some of the most sought-after professionals with very high salaries. Once again, I felt like I had missed the trend.

But things change quickly.

AI is increasing productivity in tech so fast that many companies are now restructuring and reducing staff. At the same time, fewer students are choosing civil engineering. This may create the opposite situation. In the next 10–20 years, the construction industry may face a serious shortage of engineers — and it may also be one of the hardest industries for AI to fully replace.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗔𝗜 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰𝘂𝗹𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝗱𝗲𝗲𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝗻 𝗰𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗹 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 & 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴?
AI works best in fields that have two characteristics:
- Large and accessible data
- Highly repetitive problems
This is why AI is advancing very fast in areas such as:
- software development
- translation
- graphic design
- content creation
- data analysis
These industries have huge amounts of data on the internet: GitHub, StackOverflow, images, videos, audio, documents. 
𝑨𝑰 𝒄𝒂𝒏 𝒍𝒆𝒂𝒓𝒏 𝒇𝒓𝒐𝒎 𝒃𝒊𝒍𝒍𝒊𝒐𝒏𝒔 𝒐𝒇 𝒆𝒙𝒂𝒎𝒑𝒍𝒆𝒔.
But construction is different.
In this industry, technical data is rarely public. Design documents, structural calculations, geotechnical data, and construction methods usually belong to consulting firms, contractors, or project owners. 
𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗹𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗻𝗼 𝗺𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗼 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺.

AI can help engineers:
- calculate faster
- check errors
- optimize some parameters
𝑩𝒖𝒕 𝒇𝒖𝒍𝒍𝒚 𝒓𝒆𝒑𝒍𝒂𝒄𝒊𝒏𝒈 𝒅𝒆𝒔𝒊𝒈𝒏 𝒆𝒏𝒈𝒊𝒏𝒆𝒆𝒓𝒔 𝒊𝒔 𝒔𝒕𝒊𝒍𝒍 𝒗𝒆𝒓𝒚 𝒗𝒆𝒓𝒚 𝒇𝒂𝒓 𝒂𝒘𝒂𝒚.

What about construction on site?
If office work can be partially supported by AI, construction on site is a completely different story. Planning construction methods is not only a technical problem. It also involves: safety, real site conditions, practical experience
One wrong decision can affect the entire structure and even human lives.
In the near future, AI may help in some areas such as:
- site monitoring using computer vision
- schedule analysis
- risk prediction
But the decisions will still depend on experienced engineers.

𝗔𝗜 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘆, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗶𝘁 𝗺𝘂𝗰𝗵 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀.

𝐂𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐥 𝐄𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐯𝐬 𝐈𝐓: 𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐈𝐬 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫

Recently, I spoke with some friends working in AI, and they asked an interesting question: Is civil engineering hard, and how should we think about career paths for our kids given recent AI layoffs?
It made me reflect, and I’d like to share a few simple thoughts.

●  𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞
Civil engineering is experience-driven. Most knowledge is built on previous generations, so key roles usually come after many years of practice, often in the 50s or 60s.
In contrast, IT allows faster growth. Talented individuals can stand out early, even during university.

●  𝐖𝐚𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠
Being good at math and logic is important, especially in IT. However, for engineering, that is not enough.
A good engineer is usually someone who observes the real world. When they see a structure, they naturally ask questions like: “Why is it designed this way?” or “Why not another solution?” This habit of observing and questioning is what really builds strong engineering thinking.

●  𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐜𝐨𝐩𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞
From a practical point of view, IT has a much larger scale. A software product can reach millions or billions of users, grow quickly, and create very high income potential without a clear limit.
In contrast, civil engineering projects, like bridges, have high value but serve a specific region, so the financial ceiling is more limited.

● 𝐃𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐲
If you are a person who loves very hard challenges, civil engineering may not always satisfy you in the same way as some other fields.
I once told my wife, who is a biotechnology researcher, something like this: I can explain to you many of the things you see in front of your eyes — things that are extremely large, like very tall buildings or bridges reaching into the sky — things so big that humans look tiny compared to them.
And she replied with a very simple but very sharp point: 
𝑻𝒉𝒆 𝒕𝒉𝒊𝒏𝒈𝒔 𝒚𝒐𝒖 𝒄𝒂𝒏 𝒔𝒆𝒆 𝒂𝒏𝒅 𝒆𝒙𝒑𝒍𝒂𝒊𝒏 𝒂𝒓𝒆 𝒐𝒇𝒕𝒆𝒏 𝒔𝒊𝒎𝒑𝒍𝒆𝒓 𝒕𝒉𝒂𝒏 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒕𝒉𝒊𝒏𝒈𝒔 𝒚𝒐𝒖 𝒄𝒂𝒏𝒏𝒐𝒕 𝒔𝒆𝒆 𝒃𝒖𝒕 𝒔𝒕𝒊𝒍𝒍 𝒉𝒂𝒗𝒆 𝒕𝒐 𝒊𝒎𝒂𝒈𝒊𝒏𝒆 𝒂𝒏𝒅 𝒆𝒙𝒑𝒍𝒂𝒊𝒏. ☺

When I thought about it again, I realized she was right.
☛ Many of the hardest problems today are not the big things we can see, but the very small ones—like semiconductors, precision materials, or cell structures.

✔ In general, technology will continue to improve productivity across all industries, so IT will always remain a core field. At the same time, as long as humans exist, civil engineering will always be essential, as we will always need infrastructure to live, move, and build our world.
However, in the future, IT alone may not be enough, it becomes much more valuable when combined with another expertise.

𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐖𝐚𝐫 𝐭𝐨 𝐄𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠: 𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐅𝐄𝐌 𝐖𝐚𝐬 𝐁𝐨𝐫𝐧

The world is entering unstable times again. And once more, we are seeing some of the most advanced technologies come to light.

It is a bit ironic — 𝒎𝒂𝒏𝒚 𝒐𝒇 𝒕𝒉𝒆𝒔𝒆 𝒕𝒆𝒄𝒉𝒏𝒐𝒍𝒐𝒈𝒊𝒆𝒔 𝒘𝒆𝒓𝒆 𝒏𝒐𝒕 𝒐𝒓𝒊𝒈𝒊𝒏𝒂𝒍𝒍𝒚 𝒅𝒆𝒗𝒆𝒍𝒐𝒑𝒆𝒅 𝒇𝒐𝒓 𝒅𝒂𝒊𝒍𝒚 𝒍𝒊𝒇𝒆, 𝒃𝒖𝒕 𝒇𝒐𝒓 𝒘𝒂𝒓.

A simple example is GPS. Civilian accuracy is a few meters, while military systems can reach centimeters. This gap shows that the most advanced technologies are often kept as national secrets before becoming public.

In our civil engineering field, there is something many people may not realize: 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐅𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐄𝐥𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐝 (𝐅𝐄𝐌), one of the most important tools we use today, also has roots in military needs.

During World War II, the aerospace industry developed very quickly. Engineers had to design aircraft wings that were both light and strong, able to handle complex loads, vibration, and aerodynamic forces.

So engineers came up with a new idea:
Instead of trying to solve the whole structure at once, they divided it into many small, simpler pieces, solved each part, and then connected everything together.

That idea became the foundation of FEM. It started from practical needs during wartime and was developed into a complete method in the following decades.

𝐅𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐄𝐥𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐝 (𝐅𝐄𝐌)
Imagine a large structure, we do something very simple: We break it into many small pieces.
◉ Each small piece has its own behavior. It reacts to forces depending on: material, shape and size
◉ And these pieces are not independent. They are connected at points called nodes. And at these nodes, there is an important rule: All connected pieces must move together. They cannot separate or behave differently.
Also, at boundaries (like supports), movement can be fixed or limited.

Because of all these connections and constraints, the structure cannot deform freely. Everything must satisfy all conditions at the same time.
To make that happen, we build and solve a very large system of equations.
🔷 It is a 𝐒𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦 𝐨𝐟 𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐄𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

This is the only way to ensure that all parts “agree” with each other.
Once we solve it, we get the displacement, then we can calculate stress, strain, and internal forces.
It can be used for almost anything — 1D, 2D, 3D problems. It can handle complex shapes and combine different physical effects like mechanics, heat, and fluid flow.
And most importantly, computers can handle the huge system of equations behind it.

► 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐭’𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐲 𝐢𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐨𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐧 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 “𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐲 𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐥” 𝐨𝐫 “𝐦𝐚𝐠𝐢𝐜 𝐭𝐨𝐨𝐥” 𝐨𝐟 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐮𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐦𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐜𝐬.

Just a random thought about engineering and FEM while watching the world change again.

If you love bridges, you should visit the Yeosu–Goheung island-connecting bridge route at least once. There are not many places in the world where you can see so many large sea bridges connected in one route.
This route is often described as an open-air “bridge museum.” It includes a total of 11 sea bridges connecting many islands. Together, they create a magnificent landscape where nature and human engineering meet. 

In the Hwatae–Baegya section alone, there are four long-span bridges. Our company ENVICO and Kwansoo E&C participated in the design of these bridges, and they are now under construction. 
What makes this section special is that each bridge has a different structural type, such as a suspension bridge, cable-stayed bridges, and a steel arch bridge. They are also built using different construction methods. Because of this, the whole route feels like a large bridge exhibition standing in the middle of the sea. 

I believe this is also one of the main purposes of this investment. These bridges are not only built to connect islands. They are also built to become landmarks, to create new value for tourism, local economy, and the landscape of each island. 

From above, the bridges connecting the islands look like a continuous masterpiece where nature and human bridge engineering come together.
(See the photo in the comments.)

Ten years ago (1st picture), I drove along the Changseon–Samcheonpo Bridge route. This route also felt like an open-air bridge museum, with several great bridges created by engineers of that time. I still remember how overwhelmed I felt when I was crossing one bridge and could already see another huge bridge standing ahead. It was impressive, exciting, and made me deeply respect the engineers who turned the sea, islands, and long distances into one continuous journey. 

And today, in 2026, I am here again. This time, I am standing at the construction site of another open-air bridge museum. It is still being completed, but it already feels even larger and more impressive than the one I visited years ago. 

I am not only here as a visitor. I am also here with pride, seeing what our company is helping to create: a powerful and unique combination of bridges that is not easy to find in many places in the world. 

For an engineer, happiness can be very simple. It is the moment when drawings, numbers, and technical calculations slowly become real structures standing between the sea and the sky. 

Thank you.

I recently took an automated subway and sat in the very front.

For the first time, I could clearly see inside the tunnel.

It was not dark or mysterious at all.

There were lights, walkways for workers, maintenance areas, control rooms, and many other systems along the way.

Everything was clear and organized.

It made me think about AI vibe coding in engineering.

For engineers who only use software, the software can feel like a subway tunnel.

You get on at point A, enter some inputs, and hope the software takes you safely to point B.

You may not really know what is happening inside.

But if you develop engineering software, you need to understand the tunnel.

With AI and vibe coding, you do not need to enter every control room or operate every system yourself.

AI can handle many of those details.

But you still need to walk through the tunnel.

You need to know what each part does, where the important control points are, and how everything connects.

Then the system is no longer a black box.

If the train stops somewhere, you know where it stopped and why.

You are not just sitting inside, hoping it will reach the destination without any problems.

I think this is how engineers should approach AI vibe coding:

You don’t need to control every detail yourself.
But you need to understand the whole system.

#AI #vibecoding
